text.p: Following are some of the historical events which took place on October 23.

42 BC - Marcus Junius Brutus, a leader in the plot to assassinate Julius Caesar, committed suicide when his republican cause was lost and he was heavily defeated in the battle of Philippi by Antony and Octavian.
1642 - The Battle of Edgehill was fought, the first major conflict of the English Civil War between the royalists under King Charles I and the Parliamentarians. Both sides claimed victory.
1817 - Pierre Athanase Larousse born. French lexicographer and encyclopaedist whose most notable accomplishment was the "Grand Dictionnaire Universel du XIX Siecle."
1915 - Physician and cricketer William Gilbert (W.G.) Grace died. In a first class career which lasted from 1868 to 1908 he made 126 centuries and scored almost 55,000 runs.
1917 - In World War One, the Battle of Caporetto began. A pivotal conflict between the Austrians and Germans and the Italians, who lost almost 100,000 prisoners on the first day.
1922 - Shortest term of office this century for a British prime minister began when Andrew Bonar Law took office. Due to ill health he was replaced on 22 May 1923 by Stanley Baldwin.
1940 - Brazilian footballer Pele was born and christened as Edson Arantes do Nascimento. He made his international debut at 16 and appeared in two World Cup finals of 1958 and 1970.
1942 - British and Commonwealth forces led by General Bernard Montgomery launched a huge offensive against German and Italian forces under Rommel at El Alamein, Egypt.
1950 - Al Jolson, who described himself as the "world's greatest entertainer", died. A stage performer since 1899, he starred in the first talking picture, "The Jazz Singer", in 1927.

1954 - After a series of conferences in Paris, Britain, the United States, France and the Soviet Union agreed to end the occupation of Germany. Other accords set up the Western European Union and allowed for West German entry into NATO.
1956 - The Hungarian national uprising against Soviet occupation began with students and workers demonstrating in Budapest.
1958 - Russian author Boris Pasternak was awarded the Nobel Prize for literature for "Doctor Zhivago," a best-selling novel in the West but not then published in his own country.

1961 - Dag Hammarskjoeld, former secretary-general of the United Nations, was posthumously awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. The delayed Nobel Peace Prize for 1960 was awarded to ex-president of the African National Congress Albert Lutuli.
1973 - North Vietnamese negotiator Le Duc Tho refused to accept the Nobel Peace Prize, saying there was still no peace in his country.
1980 - Alexei Kosygin resigned as Soviet prime minister due to ill health. He was replaced by Nikolai Tikhonov.
1983 - Shi'ite Moslem suicide bombers blew up the U.S. and French headquarters in Beirut, killing 241 U.S marines and 58 French paratroopers.
1990 - Ukrainian Prime Minister Vitaly Masol resigned after mass student protests, the first Soviet official of his rank to quit under public pressure.
1990 - Iraq announced freedom for all 330 French captives held in the Gulf crisis, along with 33 mainly sick or aged Britons and 14 Americans.
1995 - U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin agreed that Russia would take part in a peacekeeping force to police any settlement in Bosnia.
